::: {.callout-note title="What you will learn"}
By the end of this page you should be able to:

1. choose an appropriate time-series graphic for a question;
2. distinguish trend, seasonal and cyclic patterns;
3. use seasonal plots and seasonal subseries plots to see seasonality;
4. read scatterplots, lag plots and autocorrelation plots;
5. use the white-noise ACF confidence band to judge whether an autocorrelation pattern is compatible with white noise, and understand how this supports later model-checking discussions.
:::

## Why time-series graphics matter {#sec-why}

A time series is not just a column of numbers: the order matters. A good graph can reveal patterns, unusual observations, changes over time, and relationships between variables [@r1]. In this course, those same graphics also prepare us for later tasks such as fitting models and communicating forecasts. In practice, the graph often tells you what question to ask next: *Is there a trend? Is the pattern seasonal? Is an apparent relationship linear? Are the autocorrelations compatible with white noise?*

```{dot}
//| label: fig-graphics-workflow
//| fig-cap: "A practical graphics workflow for a time series. Blue boxes are plots; orange boxes are interpretation tasks."
//| fig-alt: "Flowchart from raw time series through time plot, seasonal graphics, relationship graphics, lag and ACF diagnostics, and communication."
digraph G {
  rankdir=LR;
  bgcolor="transparent";
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=11, color="#4a78b5", fillcolor="#eef4fb"];
  edge [color="#666666", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=10];

  data [label="Ordered observations\n(y_1, ..., y_T)"];
  timeplot [label="Time plot"];
  patterns [label="Find patterns, unusual\nvalues, changes", fillcolor="#fff1d6", color="#d08b00"];
  seasonal [label="Seasonal plot or\nsubseries plot"];
  relationships [label="Scatterplot matrix\nfor variables"];
  lag [label="Lag plots"];
  acf [label="ACF plot"];
  modelcheck [label="Compare ACF with\nwhite-noise band", fillcolor="#fff1d6", color="#d08b00"];
  present [label="Present the story\non a time scale", fillcolor="#fff1d6", color="#d08b00"];

  data -> timeplot;
  timeplot -> patterns;
  patterns -> seasonal [label="fixed period?"];
  patterns -> relationships [label="other variables?"];
  patterns -> lag [label="dependence over time?"];
  lag -> acf;
  acf -> modelcheck;
  timeplot -> present;
}
```

@fig-graphics-workflow is the roadmap for the lecture: start with the time axis, then add graphics that answer more specific questions.

## Start with the time plot {#sec-time-plot}

A **time plot** puts the observation value on the vertical axis and time on the horizontal axis. The reading uses time plots as the first graphical view of a series and says that plots help identify patterns, unusual observations, changes over time, and relationships between variables [@r1].

### What to look for {#sec-look-for}

Use the first time plot to scan for three broad patterns [@r1]:

| Pattern | What it means in words | Visual clue |
|---------|-------------------------|-------------|
| **Trend** | A long-term increase or decrease; it need not be linear. | The baseline drifts upward or downward. |
| **Seasonal** | A regular pattern at fixed, known intervals such as yearly, monthly, weekly or daily. | Peaks and troughs repeat at a known period. |
| **Cyclic** | Rises and falls with no fixed frequency, often lasting two or more years and often tied to economic conditions. | Waves are visible, but their length changes. |

: Three time-series patterns named in the reading {#tbl-patterns tbl-colwidths="[20,45,35]"}

::: {.callout-warning title="Seasonal is not the same as cyclic"}
A seasonal pattern has a fixed, known period. A cyclic pattern has rises and falls but no fixed frequency [@r1].
:::

### Interactive explorer: build a time plot (our example) {#sec-explorer}

The next figure is an illustration, not data from the reading. Move the controls and watch how the same time plot can show trend, seasonality, both, or neither.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof ts_controls = Inputs.form({
  trend: Inputs.range([-0.8, 0.8], {value: 0.25, step: 0.05, label: "Trend strength"}),
  amplitude: Inputs.range([0, 8], {value: 4, step: 0.5, label: "Seasonal amplitude"}),
  noise: Inputs.range([0, 4], {value: 1.2, step: 0.2, label: "Extra non-seasonal movement"})
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| label: fig-time-explorer
//| fig-cap: "A synthetic time series showing how trend, a period-12 seasonal wave and extra non-seasonal movement change the time plot."
//| fig-alt: "Interactive line chart with sliders for trend, seasonal amplitude, and irregular movement."
ts_points = d3.range(1, 49).map((t) => ({
  t,
  y: 20 + ts_controls.trend * t + ts_controls.amplitude * Math.sin(2 * Math.PI * t / 12) + ts_controls.noise * Math.sin(2.35 * t + 0.4)
}))

Plot.plot({
  height: 320,
  x: {label: "time t"},
  y: {label: "value y_t", grid: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleY([20], {stroke: "#bbbbbb"}),
    Plot.line(ts_points, {x: "t", y: "y", stroke: "steelblue", strokeWidth: 2}),
    Plot.dot(ts_points, {x: "t", y: "y", fill: "steelblue", r: 2})
  ]
})
```

In @fig-time-explorer, a non-zero trend tilts the long-run level; a larger seasonal amplitude makes the period-12 wave clearer; extra non-seasonal movement makes that period-12 pattern harder to see.

::: {#exm-first-read}
## First read of a time plot (our example)
Suppose the time plot in @fig-time-explorer uses trend strength $0.25$, seasonal amplitude $4$, and irregular movement $1.2$.

**Step 1. Check long-run direction.** The baseline rises as $t$ increases, so the example contains an upward trend.

**Step 2. Check repetition.** The wave repeats about every $12$ observations, so the example contains seasonality with period $12$.

**Step 3. Check extra movement.** Points do not sit exactly on the period-12 wave, so there is additional non-seasonal movement too.

**Check.** If you set seasonal amplitude to $0$, the period-12 wave disappears while the trend remains. That confirms the two features are different.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Check yourself"}
1. If monthly data have a repeating annual pattern, what seasonal period would you expect?
2. If a series rises and falls in waves of unequal length, should you first call that seasonal or cyclic?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answers"}
1. $12$, because there are 12 months in a year.
2. Cyclic, because the frequency is not fixed. If the period becomes fixed and known, then it is seasonal.
:::

## Choose the seasonal scale {#sec-seasonal-scale}

Seasonality requires a time unit and a period. The reading lists common seasonal periods for different data frequencies [@r1]. A few entries are enough to build intuition:

| Data frequency | Natural seasonal period | Example interpretation |
|----------------|-------------------------|------------------------|
| Quarterly | $4$ per year | Q1, Q2, Q3, Q4 repeat each year. |
| Monthly | $12$ per year | January through December repeat each year. |
| Weekly | $52$ per year | Week-of-year pattern. |
| Daily | $7$ per week or $365.25$ per year | Day-of-week or day-of-year pattern. |
| Hourly | $24$ per day or $168$ per week | Hour-of-day or hour-of-week pattern. |

: Common seasonal periods from the reading {#tbl-seasonal-periods tbl-colwidths="[25,30,45]"}

A single series can have more than one plausible seasonal scale. For example, daily data may be explored with a weekly period ($7$) or a yearly period ($365.25$), and hourly data may be explored with daily ($24$), weekly ($168$), or yearly ($8766$) periods [@r1]. The reading's "multiple seasonal periods" examples are a reminder to choose the period from the question, not only from the data frequency.

### Seasonal plots {#sec-seasonal-plots}

A **seasonal plot** plots the data against time *within* each seasonal period. It is useful for identifying seasonal patterns and anomalies, and can be used for multiple seasonal periods [@r1].

```{dot}
//| label: fig-seasonal-rearrange
//| fig-cap: "How a seasonal plot rearranges a series: the same observations are grouped by position inside each season."
//| fig-alt: "Diagram showing a chronological series split into years and arranged by quarter within each year."
digraph G {
  rankdir=LR;
  bgcolor="transparent";
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=11, color="#4a78b5", fillcolor="#eef4fb"];
  edge [color="#666666", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=10];

  chron [label="Chronological order\nYear 1: Q1 Q2 Q3 Q4\nYear 2: Q1 Q2 Q3 Q4"];
  split [label="Split by seasonal period\n(period = 4)", fillcolor="#fff1d6", color="#d08b00"];
  seasonal [label="Seasonal plot\nx-axis: Q1, Q2, Q3, Q4\nline/color: year"];
  compare [label="Compare the same\nseason across years", fillcolor="#fff1d6", color="#d08b00"];

  chron -> split -> seasonal -> compare;
}
```

@fig-seasonal-rearrange shows the key move: keep the values, but change the horizontal axis from absolute time to within-season time.

### Seasonal subseries plots {#sec-subseries}

A **seasonal subseries plot** collects the data for each season together as separate time series. The reading says this makes the underlying seasonal pattern clear and lets changes in seasonality over time be visualized [@r1].

| Plot | Horizontal comparison | Best question |
|------|------------------------|---------------|
| Time plot | Observation time | What happens overall? |
| Seasonal plot | Position within the season | Do years or cycles have the same within-season shape? |
| Seasonal subseries plot | Time within one named season | Is January changing differently from July? |

: Time plot, seasonal plot and seasonal subseries plot compared {#tbl-seasonal-graphics tbl-colwidths="[25,35,40]"}

::: {#exm-seasonal-choice}
## Choosing a seasonal graphic (our example)
You have quarterly tourism data and suspect Q3 behaves differently from the other quarters.

**Step 1. Identify the period.** Quarterly data have period $4$ per year, from @tbl-seasonal-periods.

**Step 2. Start with a time plot.** This checks the overall trend and unusual observations.

**Step 3. Add a seasonal plot.** Put Q1--Q4 on the x-axis and draw one line per year to see the repeated quarterly shape.

**Step 4. Add a seasonal subseries plot.** Collect all Q3 values together to see whether Q3 is changing over time.

**Check.** The seasonal plot answers "within a year, which quarter is high?" The subseries plot answers "within a quarter, is the level changing across years?"
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it"}
For hourly data, which plot would you use first to compare Monday 09:00 with Tuesday 09:00 patterns: a simple time plot, a seasonal plot with a daily period, or a seasonal subseries plot with an hour-of-week grouping?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Use a seasonal subseries-style grouping by hour of week if the goal is to compare named positions such as Monday 09:00 and Tuesday 09:00 over time. A daily seasonal plot can reveal hour-of-day shape, but it mixes weekdays unless you also separate by day.
:::

## Relationships between variables: scatterplots and correlation {#sec-relationships}

When there is more than one variable, the reading introduces scatterplots, correlation, and scatterplot matrices [@r1]. A **scatterplot** puts one variable on each axis; a **scatterplot matrix** repeats this idea for several pairs of variables.

The reading defines correlation as a measure of the extent of a linear relationship between two variables [@r1]. For paired observations $(x_t,y_t)$, the sample correlation is

$$
r=\frac{\sum\left(x_t-\bar{x}\right)\left(y_t-\bar{y}\right)}{\sqrt{\sum\left(x_t-\bar{x}\right)^2} \sqrt{\sum\left(y_t-\bar{y}\right)^2}}.
$$ {#eq-correlation}

Here $x_t$ and $y_t$ are the paired values at time $t$, while $\bar{x}$ and $\bar{y}$ are their sample means.

::: {.callout-warning title="Correlation sees linear association"}
The reading illustrates that correlation measures linear relationship; therefore a scatterplot is still needed to see shape, outliers, and non-linear structure [@r1].
:::

::: {#exm-correlation}
## Calculating a small correlation (our example)
Take three paired observations: $(x,y)=(1,2),(2,4),(3,5)$.

**Step 1. Compute means.** $\bar{x}=2$ and $\bar{y}=\frac{11}{3}$.

**Step 2. Compute centered values.** For $x$: $-1,0,1$. For $y$: $-\frac{5}{3},\frac{1}{3},\frac{4}{3}$.

**Step 3. Use @eq-correlation.**

$$
\begin{aligned}
r
&=\frac{(-1)(-5/3)+0(1/3)+1(4/3)}{\sqrt{(-1)^2+0^2+1^2}\sqrt{(-5/3)^2+(1/3)^2+(4/3)^2}} \\
&=\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}\sqrt{42/9}}
\approx 0.982.
\end{aligned}
$$

**Check.** The value is close to $1$, matching the nearly straight increasing pattern of the three points.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Check yourself"}
If two variables have $r\approx 0$, what should you do before concluding there is "no relationship"?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Look at the scatterplot. A near-zero correlation rules out strong *linear* association, but the plot may show a curved pattern or unusual observations.
:::

## Dependence over time: lag plots and autocorrelation {#sec-acf}

A time series can be related to its own past. The reading introduces **lag plots**: each graph shows $y_t$ against $y_{t-k}$ for lag $k$ [@r1]. The autocorrelations are the correlations associated with these lag plots; for example, $r_1$ is the correlation between $y_t$ and $y_{t-1}$, and $r_2$ is the correlation between $y_t$ and $y_{t-2}$ [@r1].

For a series $y_1,\ldots,y_T$, the reading gives the autocorrelation at lag $k$ as

$$
r_k=\frac{\sum_{i\in\{k+1,\ldots,T\}}\left(y_i-\bar{y}\right)\left(y_{i-k}-\bar{y}\right)}{\sum_{i\in\{1,\ldots,T\}}\left(y_i-\bar{y}\right)^2},
$$ {#eq-acf}

where $\bar{y}$ is the sample mean and $T$ is the length of the series [@r1].

```{dot}
//| label: fig-lag-acf
//| fig-cap: "Lag plots and the ACF are two views of the same idea: compare the series with its shifted copy."
//| fig-alt: "Diagram showing y_t and a lagged y_{t-k} feeding a lag plot, then the correlation r_k, then an ACF plot over many lags."
digraph G {
  rankdir=LR;
  bgcolor="transparent";
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=11, color="#4a78b5", fillcolor="#eef4fb"];
  edge [color="#666666", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=10];

  current [label="Current values\ny_t"];
  lagged [label="Lagged values\ny_{t-k}"];
  lagplot [label="Lag plot\ny_t vs y_{t-k}", fillcolor="#fff1d6", color="#d08b00"];
  corr [label="Correlation\nr_k"];
  acf [label="ACF plot\nbar for each lag k"];

  current -> lagplot;
  lagged -> lagplot;
  lagplot -> corr;
  corr -> acf [label="repeat for k = 1, 2, ..."];
}
```

### How to read an ACF plot {#sec-read-acf}

The reading gives three key rules [@r1]:

1. when the data have trend, autocorrelations for small lags tend to be large and positive;
2. when the data are seasonal, autocorrelations tend to be large and positive at seasonal lags, such as $12$ and $24$ for monthly data with yearly seasonality;
3. when the data are both trended and seasonal, autocorrelations tend to be large and positive at small lags and at seasonal lags.

::: {#exm-acf-reading}
## Reading an ACF pattern (our example)
Suppose monthly data have large positive ACF bars at lags $1$, $2$, $12$, and $24$.

**Step 1. Interpret small lags.** Large positive values at $1$ and $2$ suggest nearby observations are similar, which is consistent with trend.

**Step 2. Interpret seasonal lags.** Large positive values at $12$ and $24$ match annual seasonality in monthly data.

**Step 3. Combine the evidence.** The ACF pattern is consistent with a trended and seasonal series.

**Check.** The seasonal period is $12$, so the repeated ACF peaks at $12$ and $24$ are exactly where @tbl-seasonal-periods tells us to look.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it"}
Weekly data show strong positive autocorrelation at lags $52$ and $104$. What pattern does this suggest?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
It suggests yearly seasonality in weekly data, because the seasonal period is about $52$ weeks, and $104$ is two such periods.
:::

## White noise and the ACF confidence band {#sec-white-noise}

The reading shows white noise and its ACF, then states that for white-noise data the sampling distribution of $r_k$ is asymptotically $N(0,1/T)$ [@r1]. Therefore an approximate 95% confidence interval for $r_k$ is

$$
\pm \frac{1.96}{\sqrt{T}},
$$ {#eq-acf-ci}

where $T$ is the length of the series [@r1].

**Syllabus bridge.** The reading-supported fact is the white-noise ACF distribution and band in @eq-acf-ci. When later lectures ask whether a fitted model has left time dependence behind, this is the graphical ingredient to remember: an ACF pattern compatible with white noise should have most bars inside the approximate band. This page does not add a full residual-diagnostics procedure because the reading does not give one.

::: {#exm-ci}
## ACF band width (our example)
A series has length $T=100$.

**Step 1. Substitute into @eq-acf-ci.**

$$
\frac{1.96}{\sqrt{100}}=\frac{1.96}{10}=0.196.
$$

**Step 2. Interpret.** The approximate 95% white-noise band is from $-0.196$ to $0.196$.

**Step 3. Use visually.** A lag with $r_k=0.40$ lies outside this band; a lag with $r_k=0.05$ lies inside it.

**Check.** If $T$ increases, $\sqrt{T}$ increases, so the band becomes narrower.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Check yourself"}
For white noise with $T=400$, what is the approximate 95% ACF band?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$1.96/\sqrt{400}=1.96/20=0.098$, so the band is approximately $[-0.098,0.098]$.
:::

## Presenting forecasting results starts with the same graphics {#sec-forecast-presentation}

The syllabus asks you to present forecasting results. This reading does not give a separate forecast-display recipe. What it does give is the graphical vocabulary that a later forecast display will reuse: time plots, seasonal periods, anomalies, relationships and ACF checks [@r1]. The course-level bridge is simple: when communicating future values, keep the historical time scale and the relevant patterns visible, but treat this as an application of the reading's graphics rather than a forecast rule stated in the reading.

```{dot}
//| label: fig-forecast-bridge
//| fig-cap: "How the graphics in this lecture prepare a forecast presentation."
//| fig-alt: "Concept map connecting exploration, model checking and forecast communication."
digraph G {
  rankdir=TB;
  bgcolor="transparent";
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=11, color="#4a78b5", fillcolor="#eef4fb"];
  edge [color="#666666", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=10];

  explore [label="Explore\ntime plot, seasonal plots"];
  features [label="Name features\ntrend, seasonality, cycles"];
  check [label="Check dependence\nlag plots and ACF"];
  communicate [label="Communicate forecasts\non the same time scale", fillcolor="#fff1d6", color="#d08b00"];

  explore -> features;
  features -> check;
  check -> communicate;
  explore -> communicate [label="show history clearly"];
}
```

@fig-forecast-bridge is deliberately conservative: it connects this lecture's plots to forecast communication without adding methods that are not in the reading.

::: {.callout-note title="Check yourself"}
You are preparing to communicate future monthly values for a series with clear annual seasonality. Which feature from this lecture should remain visible in the historical part of the display?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Keep the time scale and the annual seasonal pattern visible. Monthly data with yearly seasonality have period $12$, so the viewer should be able to compare future values with the repeating pattern seen in the historical time plot or seasonal graphics.
:::

```{dot}
  graphics -> time;
  graphics -> seasonal;
  graphics -> scatter;
  graphics -> lag;
  lag -> acf;
  time -> trend;
  time -> season;
  time -> cycle;

```

A good workflow is to move from broad to specific: use a time plot first, seasonal graphics when the period matters, scatterplots when variables relate, and lag/ACF graphics when dependence over time matters.

## Summary {#sec-summary}

::: {.callout-important title="What to remember"}
- Time plots are the starting point: they reveal patterns, unusual observations and changes over time.
- Trend is long-term increase or decrease; seasonality repeats at a fixed known period; cyclic movement does not have a fixed frequency.
- Seasonal plots compare positions within a season; seasonal subseries plots collect each season as its own small time series.
- Correlation measures linear relationship, so always read it with a scatterplot.
- Lag plots compare $y_t$ with $y_{t-k}$; the ACF records those correlations across many lags.
- Trend tends to create large positive ACF at small lags; seasonality tends to create large positive ACF at seasonal lags.
- For white noise, an approximate 95% ACF band is $\pm 1.96/\sqrt{T}$.
:::

## Key terms {#sec-key-terms}

| Term | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| Time plot | A plot of a series value against time; the first view for patterns and unusual observations. |
| Trend | Long-term increase or decrease in the data; not necessarily linear. |
| Seasonal pattern | A regular pattern at fixed, known intervals such as yearly, monthly, weekly or daily. |
| Cyclic pattern | Rises and falls without fixed frequency, often lasting two or more years. |
| Seasonal period | The number of observations in one full repeating seasonal cycle, such as $12$ for monthly yearly seasonality. |
| Seasonal plot | A plot against time within each seasonal period, useful for seeing seasonal patterns and anomalies. |
| Seasonal subseries plot | A display that collects each season together as a separate time series to show seasonal pattern and change. |
| Scatterplot | A two-variable plot used to see relationships between variables. |
| Correlation | A measure of the extent of linear relationship between two variables. |
| Lag plot | A plot of $y_t$ against $y_{t-k}$ for a chosen lag $k$. |
| Autocorrelation | The correlation between a series and a lagged version of itself. |
| ACF plot | A plot of autocorrelations $r_k$ across several lags. |
| White noise | The benchmark series used in the reading for ACF confidence bands; its $r_k$ has approximate distribution $N(0,1/T)$. |

: Key terms for time-series graphics {#tbl-key-terms tbl-colwidths="[28,72]"}
